text: Eradication and restoring a clean backup feel like the finish line — the malware's gone, the root cause is supposedly patched, the database is back from a known-good copy. Real IR practice treats that as one phase short of done. Validation is the checkpoint between cleanup and production, and it catches problems that don't show up until a system is live again.

Meridian's SOC runs four specific checks before either server goes back into production, and none of them is just 'it looks fine now.' Patch confirmation, a persistence re-check on every host, a vulnerability scan targeted at the exact weakness exploited, and a defined window of elevated monitoring before the incident is formally closed.

Get-HotFix confirms the security update is actually installed and active, not just scheduled or sitting in a deployment queue. That distinction matters because a pending or failed patch install can look identical to a successful one from the outside — nothing about the server's normal behavior changes either way.

The same scheduled task, local user, and registry checks from Lesson 17 run again here, on every host in scope, expecting no results this time. Eradication work finished under time pressure is exactly the kind of work worth re-verifying, rather than trusting entirely on the first pass before the system goes live again.

Rushing or skipping validation is a common, well-documented real mistake, and it rarely looks dramatic in the moment — just a tight timeline and a restore that already looked clean. The cost shows up later: the same vulnerability gets re-exploited, or a missed foothold reactivates, and now it's the same incident reopening on a team that believed it was closed.

A 72-hour monitoring window, with detection rules tuned to the attacker's observed behavior, exists specifically to catch that failure mode while it's still small instead of a month later. Next: once validation passes, how systems actually come back online — gradually, in phases, not all turned back on at once.
